messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame Mensah, a 77-year-old African American man who had spent most of his life in the United States after arriving as a refugee, came to treatment because his world had gradually narrowed to the point that even a routine outing felt charged. He worked part-time as a software engineer from home, but over the past several years he had found himself avoiding people and rarely going out except when absolutely necessary. His wife had begun to notice that he kept his mind occupied constantly, moving from one screen, crossword, or technical article to another, as though any unstructured moment might leave him exposed to something he could not manage. Kwame described this as more than shyness: when someone gave him a firm instruction, or when he heard news, voices, or images that reminded him of the turmoil he had fled, a wave of unease would rise so quickly that he would feel himself beginning to detach, almost unreal, as if he were not fully in the room.

The traumatic period he referred to was a time of raids, shouted commands, and sudden flight, when he had been ordered about by armed men and had to move his family with no certainty of where safety lay. What stayed with him from those days was not a continuous story but a series of pictures: a doorway, a pair of boots, his children’s faces in a half-lit room, the flash of a street corner at night. He said he could sometimes recall what happened, but it came to him numb and distant, like it had happened to a stranger. The memories arrived in snapshots rather than a sequence, and that fragmentary quality made them feel even more vivid in some moments and strangely blank in others. When he was reminded of the trauma by current events, especially anything that resembled commands or orders, the images would return with force and leave him unsettled, and he had come to dread that loss of steadiness enough to pull away from situations where such reminders might appear.

Over time, those reminders shaped his habits. If he had to go out, he would plan everything obsessively and often cancel at the last minute; if he could avoid people, he did. He had arranged his life so that errands could be done early, quickly, and with as little contact as possible. At work, even though he remained skilled and proud of his long career, he increasingly preferred email to conversation and found meetings tiring if someone else directed the discussion too forcefully. Yet his attempts to keep busy and keep away from reminders did not settle him for long. The more he filled his attention, the more his memory seemed to return in those isolated images, and with them the same old feeling that he was once again under someone else’s command. A neighborhood police siren, a stern tone from a cashier, or a televised scene of people being ordered to move could turn a normal day into one of suspicion and withdrawal, because the memory itself had become linked to those present-day cues. At the same time, his effort to stay away from people and stay indoors meant he encountered fewer ordinary corrections to that fear; in the quiet of home, with little to distract him except his own thoughts, the pictures grew sharper and more intrusive, and he found himself even more determined to avoid going out or engaging with others.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had begun to strain his marriage and reduce his confidence in daily life. His wife worried that he was disappearing into avoidance and constant mental busyness, while Kwame felt embarrassed by how fragile he became when an instruction was delivered in a certain tone or when a brief image on the news echoed his past. He was not seeking relief from a single flash of memory so much as from the way those moments had come to dominate his choices. What frightened him most was the sense that he could be pulled back into that same detached, numb state at any time, and he hoped treatment might help him stay present enough to go out again, be with people, and live without organizing every hour around the threat of another image, another command, or another disappearance from himself.
